prompt.en: A portable kit has a lithium-based pack from another hobby. Which compatibility check is sufficient before using it in the station?

text.en: Check its specified charger, protection, connection method, and suitability for the radio load.

feedback.en: The pack design and chemistry govern charging and protection as well as the station connection. Follow the specified system and load ratings.

text.en: Treat matching connector fit and nominal voltage as sufficient for this pack.

feedback.en: Those checks do not establish suitable charging, protection, or load behaviour for a lithium-based pack.

text.en: Treat adequate transmit-current capability as sufficient, even with a charger from a different battery type.

feedback.en: Load capability and charging compatibility are different checks. A charger must suit the pack's chemistry and specifications.

text.en: Use the existing charger if its nominal voltage matches, since that is a reasonable chemistry check.

feedback.en: Equal nominal voltage does not establish compatible chemistry or charge control. Use the pack's specified charging method.

explanation.en: Battery compatibility includes chemistry, protection, load capability, polarity, and approved connection and charging methods. No single label or connector establishes all of them.

prompt.en: A battery station draws twice the planned transmit current. In a simple model, source voltage and lead resistance stay fixed. What happens at the radio input?

text.en: The voltage drop doubles and radio input voltage rises.

feedback.en: The drop does double, but it is subtracted from source voltage. The radio receives less voltage, not more.

text.en: The voltage drop stays fixed because the same leads are installed.

feedback.en: Resistance stayed fixed, not voltage drop. By E = I x R, more current causes more drop.

text.en: The voltage drop doubles and radio input voltage falls.

feedback.en: At fixed resistance, doubling current doubles the lead drop. More of the source voltage is lost in the leads.

text.en: The voltage drop halves and radio input voltage rises.

feedback.en: This reverses the current relationship. Fixed resistance gives a larger drop at larger current.

explanation.en: At fixed resistance, lead voltage drop follows current. Greater drop leaves less of the source voltage available at the radio.

prompt.en: A switching supply rated 30 A powers a 19 A radio. DC voltage is correct at idle and during transmit. Which further check addresses remaining signal-quality risks?

text.en: Check receiver and transmitted noise with the supply installed and loaded.

feedback.en: Adequate current does not prove RF quietness. Test the installed station under relevant receive and transmit loads.

text.en: Confirm again that the printed current rating exceeds 19 A.

feedback.en: This rechecks current headroom, not RF noise. Both are needed for a useful station supply.

text.en: Accept the idle voltage check as a useful substitute for an RF noise test.

feedback.en: Correct idle DC voltage does not establish clean receiver or transmitter operation with the supply installed.

text.en: Accept steady loaded DC voltage as evidence that switching noise is adequately suppressed.

feedback.en: Good regulation and RF cleanliness are different properties. The installed supply still needs a signal-quality check.

explanation.en: A station supply must have adequate voltage and current and behave quietly in the installed system. A rating label cannot establish all three.
